C004.subject: Aspirin prophylaxis in adults 50–59 with elevated 10-year cardiovascular risk and low bleeding risk
C004.object: nonfatal myocardial infarction risk only when combined with a proton pump inhibitor
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Aspirin prophylaxis in adults 50–59 with elevated 10-year cardiovascular risk and low bleeding risk nonfatal myocardial infarction risk only when combined with a proton pump inhibitor]

[PATH:empirical] Post-hoc analysis of ARRIVE trial data stratifying by concomitant PPI use and bleeding events — Re-analyzing the ARRIVE trial, which excluded high-risk patients and did not mandate gastroprotection, could reveal whether participants who happened to be on a PPI had a lower rate of upper GI bleeding and a correspondingly greater reduction in nonfatal MI, directly testing the hypothesis that bleeding offsets MI benefit.

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial of aspirin + PPI vs. aspirin alone in adults 50-59 with elevated 10-year CV risk and low bleeding risk — A dedicated RCT in the exact target subgroup, with mandatory PPI co-prescription in one arm, would provide the highest-quality evidence to confirm or refute whether gastroprotection unmasks a net MI reduction, avoiding confounding by indication present in observational analyses.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of aspirin primary prevention trials with individual-level PPI and bleeding data — Pooling individual patient data from trials like ARRIVE, ASPREE, and ASCEND, stratifying by PPI use and bleeding outcomes, could quantify the interaction between GI bleeding events and MI reduction, offering a theoretical and empirical basis for the hypothesized effect modification.

qualifier.tension: The ARRIVE trial excluded higher-risk patients and did not mandate gastroprotection, possibly masking a true benefit for MI reduction by allowing upper GI bleeding events to offset gains; this hypothesis proposes that co-prescribing a PPI would unmask a net benefit for MI in the target subgroup.

C005.subject: Aspirin prophylaxis in adults 50–59 with elevated 10-year cardiovascular risk
C005.object: cardiovascular event risk even when bleeding risk is low
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Aspirin prophylaxis in adults 50–59 with elevated 10-year cardiovascular risk cardiovascular event risk even when bleeding risk is low]

[PATH:empirical] Post-hoc analysis of the ASPREE trial (Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly) stratified by 10-year cardiovascular risk score in adults aged 50-59 with low bleeding risk — ASPREE is a large, placebo-controlled trial that directly tested aspirin in primary prevention. A subgroup analysis focusing on the specified age and risk stratum could provide direct evidence on whether aspirin reduces cardiovascular events when bleeding risk is low, addressing the disputed hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of individual participant data from randomized trials of aspirin in primary prevention (e.g., from the Antithrombotic Trialists' Collaboration) with stratification by age and baseline cardiovascular risk — Pooling data across trials (e.g., JPAD, POPADAD, ARRIVE) can increase statistical power to detect a modest effect in the narrow age-risk subgroup and assess heterogeneity, especially for the low-bleeding-risk subset. This would confirm or refute the null effect claim.

[PATH:empirical] Causal modeling using electronic health records from a large US healthcare system (e.g., Optum or Medicare) to emulate a target trial of aspirin initiation in adults 50-59 with elevated 10-year risk and low bleeding risk — Observational data with rigorous target trial emulation can provide real-world evidence on the net benefit of aspirin in this specific population, controlling for confounders and assessing outcomes over 2014-2024, directly testing the hypothesis in the specified geographic and temporal scope.
